Whoa! That car went from full speed to a dead stop in just a few seconds.
So how do brakes stop over a ton of metal that fast?
Step one: you press the pedal. It pushes a small piston into the master cylinder.
That squeezes the brake fluid. Fluid can't be compressed, so the push races through the lines to every wheel, instantly.
At each wheel, the fluid pushes on much bigger pistons, which multiplies your force many times over.
Those pistons clamp brake pads onto a spinning metal disc, called the rotor.
Friction turns the car's motion into heat. The rotor can get hundreds of degrees hot.
And if a wheel starts to lock up, ABS pulses the brakes many times a second, so the tyres keep gripping and you can still steer.
Pedal. Fluid. Clamp. Heat. That's how a car stops on a dime.
